utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Mr. Alexander Ivanchev from Bulgaria who has been assisting my team for the last several months. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Yes, good morning, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Kim West. I'm going to spend a little time this morning asking you some questions, and the first thing I'd like to clarify is the period of time in which you were in the Rajlovac Brigade. We know you started in May 1992, and it appears in September of 1992 you were then promoted to chief of engineers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia -- or, actually, the former JNA. When it withdrew, I stayed behind as one of the senior officers. It was myself and another commander. I was assistant commander at the time, assisting with the establishment of units in Rajlovac which were tasked to act as a buffer zone. Once the JNA left and until the 15th of September, I was in Rajlovac where I had the duty of deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your statement there are 64 substantial written paragraphs giving your evidence, and it appears that many of them refer specifically to your time in the Rajlovac Brigade. Should we understand your comments to be limited to that time or are they -- some are your comments more general in nature as applicable to the whole war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the situation was like. In that situation we were in the most difficult period during the war for the VRS. We had to start from scratch and establish units. Rajlovac as a barracks was practically empty. There were only five or six officers and between 20 and 30 workers who came to work and some assistant personnel. The rest left with the JNA units. So we need to make do. We had to get the people we could from Rajlovac and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I don't see any relationship between your answer and my question, and I don't know if this is a translation problem, but all I want to know is your comments in your statement, do these relate to only your period of time between May and September and the Rajlovac Brigade or do they apply to the whole period of the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period could be split in two parts while I was in Rajlovac. That's the first period, and the second as I was the chief of engineers in the SRK, which is between the 15th of April when I went to visit the Ilidza Brigade and until the Dayton Accords were signed when the Serbians and people withdrew from that area. I took part in that as well. Later on I participated in the process of delineation or separating the zones of responsibilities between the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska around Sarajevo. Since I was the chief of engineers, I was familiar with the situation in the field in terms of which unit was where. That is why that part of the statement probably encompasses the entire period. The initial period was critical until the units were set up alongside their commands.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So let's focus on some very specific things from your statement now. Now firstly, paragraph 42, and I know you have your statement in front of you. You can refer to it if you like, but I'll tell you what part I'm focused on. Paragraph 42, you say that the Rajlovac Brigade had no trained professional snipers. Now, for the moment, let's put aside whether you had trained professional snipers and focus on whether you had rifles that were used for sniping. Did you have such rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the army left the JNA, I need to go back to that, all quality weapons and special purpose weapons that the JNA units had were taken to Serbia. On the 10th -- or, rather, between the 10th and the 12th of May, there was a hand-over of all the assets that were left behind in Rajlovac. It was a single sheet of paper which was exchanged between the TO staff and the JNA. Major Bosnjic [phoen] received all of those assets. On behalf of the Rajlovac municipality, he was tasked with -- well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't have such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least I didn't know that we found anything like that such as sniper rifle or anything of the sort. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I appreciate your comments and I understand you're trying to give us some background. Let's first try to answer the question, and if I need more background I'll ask you. Now I understand your testimony to be we -- I didn't know that we found anything like that such as sniper rifle or anything of the sort. So I understand that it's your position that your brigade had no rifles that were used for sniping; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. I also need to add the following: Before the war there were optical devices that were being produced which could be mounted onto rifles. That is something I need to stress. There were possibilities to purchase rifles with the sights. If mounted on the rifle, one could see 2- or 300 metres more than with the naked eye, but it wasn't done. Perhaps several men had that who had that as part of their personal weapons kit. Therefore, I can't really say anything in particular, but this is sort of what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't deny that perhaps several people may have had those types of rifles with optical sights associated with them.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot deny that. I saw a few, but it wasn't a unit as a whole or anything. Now, whether such people joined the army, it was all the process of establishment, but officially speaking, in the units that were set up there were no such people, such personnel with that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness speak closer to the microphones, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, could you come closer to the microphones so that the interpreters can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has heard evidence from Prosecution expert witness that the M-76 was a standard sniper rifle and that was at transcript 6940. Do you agree with that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the optical sight was mounted, then it could be used to that end. One could even use a World War II weapon. You could use an M-48 rifle, put the optical sight on it and then visibility is increased as well as accuracy. There is such a possibility. I can't deny that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And along those same lines, the Trial Chamber heard evidence recently allowing for this possibility, as you speak of, to attach an optical sight on an M-48, and that was at transcript 31158, and I understand that you believe that to be true as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the M-76 and the M-48 were rifles, were weapons that your brigade had in its possession; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 52 and 53, this is the part of your statement that speaks about air-bombs, and it specifically -- you say that you don't know -- you don't know any details about them. You talk about technical issues, and you say you don't know about that. But in paragraph 54, you say that you had no knowledge that aerial bombs or other projectiles for ground targets were modified by the BH Army. And then at the end of the paragraph you say: "I have no knowledge about the use of modified air-bombs or other projectiles for ground targets by units of the BH Army." So just so I can understand, you never saw the BH Army use air-bombs; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. However, the shells they used to target our positions, positions of the VRS, contained shrapnel, nails, metal shavings, which increases the lethal aspect of the weapon, and it means that they produced it, they manufactured it in the part of town that was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But that's a separate issue. You've never heard -- you never had information that the BH Army was using modified air-bombs, did you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at paragraph 51, you spoke about your information regarding SRK air-bombs. You said you learned of the existence and production of modified air-bombs for ground targets which were a part of the SRK arsenal during the testing of one such air-bomb. When was that testing?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at Nisici with the corps command at the Nisici plateau, and then an aerial bomb was tested. Up until then I had no knowledge that it was being manufactured. During the test, I realised that it was just an ordinary air-bomb left behind by the JNA. It was found in the warehouses. So it happened to be in the territory of Republika Srpska or in federation territory. It was tested, and certain engines were mounted on it. I was present when one such bomb was fired. I wasn't standing at the point of where -- from where it was fired. I was on the side. But it was never launched, because the engine failed to start. Up until that point, I had no information of such bombs and that certain engines were mounted on them. It was the engines that were the most important thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like you to focus on the part up until that point. My question was when. When did the testing take place? Give me a date, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't provide you with a date. It was not in 1992. Possibly in late 1993 or in 1994, in that period. Well, one could check that against documents. I suppose it was in late 1993 or early 1994. That was the period when the first -- that first testing I saw was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And beyond this one occasion when you saw this testing, you have no other information of the SRK using aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As of that time, I had the duty of the chief of engineers in the corps, and I can't tell you, Yes, on that day an aerial bomb was used. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have P1309, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think on your screen - thank you - momentarily you're going to see a document - and you do - on the left we'll have B/C/S. And this is a document from April of 1995. This regards the action of Talas 1. You were involved with this, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wave one. It was General Milosevic who was in command at the time, the corps commander. The aim was to retake --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's stop there.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, I was tasked with --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, hold on a second. And I appreciate you wanting to give background, but let's try to first answer my question and then we'll talk about the background. So as I understand it, you were tasked for this action. So you remember this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to construct groundwork for tanks, protective barriers, and they had to be camouflaged in case there was a need to use them in the course of operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's exactly right, because we see under number 1 after the listing there's a paragraph in which it says the entire operational building resources from Major Vujasin's building site are to be engaged in organising these positions, and it goes on, and then it says they must be below ground and camouflaged. If we continue a few more paragraphs, it says: "The works shall be directed by Major Vujasin and Dusan Vukadin who will have under his command another person who are duty-bound to provide artillery pieces." So as regards this particular action, should we understood that you had real familiarity with what was going to take place overall?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically. I was tasked with setting up positions. Since I was the chief, Vukadin, Dusan was the commander of the battalion, and he had to provide assistance to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the commander, but under me. He was from a unit junior to the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But you --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very important to do that at the time, to have them camouflaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Very good.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add something. Could I just have an opportunity to explain the following: What was the reason for doing that. May I?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: A brief opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is something that you do that the enemy can see with the aim of carrying out operational camouflage. When we made the breastwork, the barriers, when the enemy could see we didn't put any tanks there. Perhaps it would drive up for it to be seen, but it wouldn't act, because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was this: It was between the 1st and the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade that each day the enemy approached our positions by some 10 to 15 metres, and the goal was to return those units to their starting position.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I think we fully understand that your task in this plan was very important. Camouflaging obviously was very important. But if we go on on the same piece -- document, a document that was sent to the Engineers Battalion, we see under number 2, and if we could go to the next page in B/C/S, please. It's the same page in English. Under number 2 this is after the part regarding your unit: "Proceed forthwith to prepare launchers and make sure that four to six aerial bombs can be launched simultaneously against the designated target, the condition being that they must hit the target, which means that provisions have to be made for more bombs so that, in the event of a miss, the next projectile lands on the target." Sir, keeping in mind your role in this attack was as we understand to be quite important, shouldn't you at the time understood that the overall tact includes aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware. We needed to make parapets. Now, whether someone indeed intended to use them, that's something I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. If we can move to paragraph 18 of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just one question. Do you know who was Tadija Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was he, and what was he responsible for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tadija Manojlovic was a retired colonel -- lieutenant-colonel in the JNA. He was with us as a volunteer who received the rank of reserve colonel in the VRS. He was the chief of artillery in the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Had he something to do with the aerial bomb at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only had to construct the parapets, and it was a way for the artillery to act, which was in his domain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Could Ms. West please slow down when speaking and reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In paragraph 18 of your statement, you indicate that the SRK mostly defended itself, but you gave an exception of offensive actions. You said that they were to improve tactical positions. And then you give an example, and your example was a tactical operation with the aim of liberating Serbian houses near Muslim positions in Sokolje when 13 people were killed. As regards to this action, was liberating Serbian houses the only aim, the only goal?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 23839, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is an order to attack. It's the Rajlovac Light Infantry Brigade, and it speaks about this attack at Sokolje. Now, this is dated November 30, 1992. Is this the attack that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it the corps command at the time? I know that Milos --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- stayed on as the commander of the brigade and he carried out preparations. This is the first time I see this. So he carried out preparations, and I know that he wanted to free or liberate Serb houses or positions where Serb houses were. As for the population from these houses, they were in the Rajlovac barracks, Bozici and others. September, November, December. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. However, we need to continue on with these questions, and let's try to focus on the question I asked, which is: Does this document represent the attack you spoke of in your statement? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I just want to go through a couple sections of this, and I'm sure you're familiar with it as you mentioned in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can have English page 2. It's B/C/S bottom of page 1. The English page 2 at the bottom. This is speaking about the enemy and what they have. It says they have very good infantry weapons but we can take advantage of the internal conflicts within their ranks to launch a fierce attack and take control of the villages. If we stay at the B/C/S -- bottom of page 1, under number 2, and then we go to the third page of the English this continues, and it says -- it talks about the task. Our brigade has been instructed to launch an attack from its starting positions, and it names the places. Cut off the village, surround the enemy forces in the village of Sokolje, and thoroughly mop up the villages, and it names the villages. And if we can now go to page 5 of the English. And it's page 2 of the B/C/S and this is under a number 5. It's talking about its task, the task of the SRK. It shall co-ordinate the activities with the strike group to take control of the line, the junction below the refuse dump, the junction of roads to Brijesko Brdo, the junction of roads, it names elevations. And then it says systematically cleanse the houses of enemy soldiers and after completing the mopping up operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, my question for you is: I've just shown you three parts of this document and clearly there's far more, but the language that we see seems to be quite aggressive. So, for example, when it says "systematically cleanse the houses of enemy soldiers," does this mean -- does this include their families as well?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see from this document that this is an attack order. According to our combat rules, that's the way it's done. An order is issued to units and to each and every individual. This never had to do with families. That's one thing. Then -- I mean, that is my understanding. If people do not put up resistance, I mean, that was the regular thing, to mop up so that there can be freedom of movement for our units. So I don't think that -- no, I don't believe, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You say: "If people do not put up resistance ... that was the regular thing, to mop up so there can be freedom of movement for our units." Do you mean that if the people, the civilians who live there, don't resist you, you then are going to force them to leave? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No, no, no. No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the fault of the interpretation and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give it a try again. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you to speak about a attack order, and then you started to talk about the procedure and the way it was done, and this is at lines 6 and 7, and you said this never had to do with families, and then what we understood you to say is if people do not put up resistance, I mean, that was the regular thing, to mop up so there was freedom of movement for our units. Please clarify exactly what you meant when you spoke about people or the families not putting up resistance.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our case and everywhere else, not opening fire, I mean, that means that that family, that unit, that house, should not be touched. There was no intention whatsoever. If somebody is not putting up resistance and not firing at the Army of Republika Srpska, they were not the enemy, and they were therefore not endangering the movements, manoeuvres of the Army of Republika Srpska. That's it. That person accepts the government organs and the system starts functioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And as regards to those people who just do nothing, do they get to stay in their house?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, they do. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I tender this document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And over here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 23839 becomes Exhibit P6067. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I want to speak about another action taken by the Rajlovac Brigade, and this is when you had just become deputy commander. It was the attack on Ahatovici. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you were the person in charge of the attack, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Or what was your position as regards the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there were village guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, sir. Stop for a second. My question is: What was your position in the Rajlovac Brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was deputy commander then, and I was at the Rajlovac barracks in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 24344, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a statement to National Security Service, and it was given in December of 1992, so the same year. It was given by an Mirko Lalic, who was a member of the Rajlovac barracks. Do you remember this person? Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I just read this?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please. Sir, I'm going to ask you a question, and --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go up a bit. Do you remember Mirko Lalic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this one Lalic. I think I know who this paper pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And he's speaking about you, and he's commenting on your successes, and he says at the bottom of page 1 in the English and 1 in the B/C/S at the time the Rajlovac Brigade performed one successful action in the Ahatovici settlement. The command of the action was the then-commander of the Rajlovac Brigade, Vujasin. So are we to understand that you had a leading role in the attack at Ahatovici?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I did not have a leading role, because when this was done, that is to say this procedure, Ahatovici, I was at a meeting in Lukavica with General Mladic; that is to say, I went there as the ranking officer in the Rajlovac Brigade at the time. So I was there, I mean, and I know full well that the orders were that not a single bullet should be fired anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because then the Butmir report was being handed over to UNPROFOR. I said to General Mladic also, I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The term did not understand what he said to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I ordered now cannot be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand that you're saying you weren't there at the time, but nonetheless, would you not consider the event at Ahatovici an offensive by the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not dare say that it was official, because this was a village with a mixed population, Serb and Muslim, so this is a hamlet of a village. So there were joint guards as I mentioned a moment ago, and, yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: As regards to who lived there, do you agree that before the war in the 1991 census there were over a thousand Muslims living in that area? And the Trial Chamber has heard evidence to this effect. Does that seem about right to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think so. It was mixed. Half/half, if you look at it. I mean, in that part and for that local commune. Now, whether there were more of one or the other, I cannot say, but I mean, Muslim Ahatovici were grouped, but these other villages, this local commune, were on the left and the right-hand side and it goes from the -- from Bosna all the way up to the hill to the pass there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has also heard evidence that by the end of the war there was only one Muslim family living in Ahatovici. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just know that the population had fled to Rajlovac and from Rajlovac into town and then wherever they wanted to go, that is to say in accordance with their own wishes. As for this family, I cannot say. I don't really know. They could have returned. Whoever wanted to could return after these unfortunate developments --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because they had this free will that they could express. However, the set of circumstances then was very difficult. Would you allow me to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No. But you can explain it if Mr. Karadzic deems it important in redirect, but let me ask you another question. Were you aware that as a result of this operation several hundred people from this settlement were detained in different places in Rajlovac? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I do know, and I barely survived, I and Mirko Krajisnik, in terms of these consequences -- may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment and let's just back up. You just said -- I asked about people being detained, and you said, as I understand it, I do know and I barely survived in terms of consequences. Are you suggesting you were detained?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me, taking care that these people do not get hurt. I'm referring to people who sought shelter in the Rajlovac barracks, from Mijatovici Brda, Zenica. These people who were expelled from Central Bosnia, they were all in barracks and officers and soldiers and families and they were all there, whereas these people had fled to our territory so we saved them and we had to provide for them. We had nowhere else to put them up so we were taking care of them so they would not be victimised in any way, and that's what happened. Fire was even opened at Mirko Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So you say that when this attacked happened, you were at a meeting elsewhere, but now I understand it that you are suggesting that when these people were detained, you had some -- some role in ensuring that they were safe. Is that what we're to understand?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saved, yes. Yes, saving these people who had fled.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, the Trial Chamber has heard evidence that a number of these people were maltreated. They were beaten. They were kept in inhumane conditions. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that they were not beaten or anything. There were situations when one individual or two would be beaten up. There was this rage. We had terrible problems to prevent that, to prevent individuals from doing that. We had terrible problems to prevent these unfortunate things happening, and these unfortunate things being done by certain individuals. I mean, people had rifles and how would I know whether they'd open a burst of gunfire at them or whatever. I mean, it wasn't good. It's not even good to think about that, about all the things that could have happened but fortunately did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And these were individuals who were subordinated to you, were they not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the barracks you cannot say that they were subordinated to me, because this was an open-type barracks. There wasn't a classical army. That is to say that units came, groups of 10 to 15 men, and then they joined up to create a brigade. And then this Mirko Lalic also, as we said, came, and then we had people, whatever, to link all of this up in that context. And now these units in Rajlovac, Ahatovici, Brijesce, all of this. I mean, it was basically the armed people. It was the people who were armed. You had to put all of this together. You could not even organise guards because 10 or 15 metres from the barracks there were Muslim forces ready to enter the barracks. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we'll move on. And if we can go to paragraph 47 of your statement. This regards gas supply to Sarajevo, which you say the gas supply to Sarajevo went through the zone of responsibility of the Rajlovac Brigade and these valves were never closed. May we have 21151, please. Sir, as I understand it, the valves that were pivotal to the gas supply in Sarajevo went through your zone of responsibility and I want to look at an UNPROFOR document that talks about that very thing. This is September of 1994. There should -- there should be a B/C/S. If the Court can bear with me, Your Honours. Sir, I will read this slowly. You're going to hear it in B/C/S. This regards what happened in September of 1994. And it says the week under review was dominated by the most lengthy and comprehensive shutdown of utilities which Sarajevo has experienced since the dark days of last winter. A combination of storm and water -- excuse me, war damage completely cut the electricity supply on 14 September. With no electricity to operate the pumps this inevitably led to the water supply into the city coming to a halt. On 15 December, the gas supply was cut. Information obtained by technical experts of this office, UNPROFOR engineering units and other sources, suggests that the gas supply was almost certainly interrupted by Bosnian Serbs closing valves in the part of the city in which they controlled. So these valves that you spoke of and this document speaks of, are those the valves in the Rajlovac zone of responsibility; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot link this up now. Where are these valves? As you move towards Olovo, I know that there was that thing that you could see, sort of a station where that could be regulated, but I think that then also the pressure was very low, because the army in Lukavica via Grbavica also had gas, so I cannot believe -- no. I don't think it was closed. So I think that it had a question of -- that it was a question of the weak flow into Republika Srpska, Bosna. That would be it. But I also know that UNPROFOR co-operated with us all the time. And may I proceed? Maybe it doesn't really have to do with this, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit more about this, but I want to go to paragraph 46 of your statement that -- just the paragraph right before and you're speaking generally about utilities. You say Karadzic's stance was to enable full and unobstructed supply of aid, water, electricity, and gas to civilians in the Muslim part of Sarajevo. What is -- what is the basis of your information for that? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Krajisnik's brother -- Momcilo Krajisnik's brother Mirko, I mean, that means that this is his brother. Momcilo was president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I found out from Mirko that their position was that there has to be this unhindered thing that people should go on living there. It's not the fault of the people if the leadership makes a mistake in some element, and this was the definite position there. That was conveyed to all, to all the people who knew that. Now, what else happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who were angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's just go to the second paragraph of this document in which it says in spite of extensive efforts being made by UNPROFOR at all appropriate levels, the week ended with gas still turned off and without --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Shall we upload that document again.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it's the second paragraph. Without the necessary clearances having been attained to enable work to begin on repairing the electricity lines. A meeting at the technical level at which this office was represented took place at the airport on the 18th. This meeting revealed that there was comparatively little disagreement between the parties on the technical problems involved, but the necessary repair work to restore the electricity and gas supplies still awaited clearance at the political level. Now, as regards to what you understood Mr. Karadzic's stance to be on the utilities, would you agree with me that he was in a position to either agree that the utilities, in this case gas, would go through, or in fact turn it off?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was not in a position to do that. This was a technical thing. Whether there was an outage or whether there was no electricity, I mean, that's what happened during the war. I can tell you one thing. For example, a wire would break down or something and then a commission would be established from both sides. This Lalic person mostly worked on this, on this combination so that there could be repairs carried out. I mean, how do I put this. Something is repaired and then within an hour again it breaks down where the separation line is. And so we didn't even get down. I mean these people would say we didn't even get down from the pole and there would be a breakdown again, and also the Muslims or whatever, I mean, intentionally. I mean, so this was done so that both sides could be accused. The station in Reljevo worked all the time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll just interrupt you there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next P exhibit, P6068.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, 65 ter 21151 shall be assigned Exhibit P6068. And for clarification of transcript only page 14, lines 20, 21, 65 ter 23839 was assigned Exhibit P6067. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to speak about your role as chief of engineers. In that role you performed work solely for the SRK; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so there were --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a professional command organ, the staff for HQ of the HQ command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during this time then, there were no occasions when you did engineering work for other entities like private companies or political communities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were working on the road from Pretis to -- from Vogosca up to Brijesce close to Pale. We were supposed to make the road. The airport was handed over to the UNPROFOR and that part of the Ilijas, Vogosca, Rajlovac, Ilidza, Hadzici municipalities was cut off from Republika Srpska. There was no road so this was a priority job, also the maintenance of the road. This was a private task, and as soon as I became deputy commander of the corps, it was my -- I gave myself this task, and we used the machinery that stayed behind in our territory. That was what we used.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please be asked to start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you overlapped with the interpretation. Please pay attention to the transcript. Could you start again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Line 9, it was translated as the witness -- as if the witness said I was a professional command organ. However, he said I was an expert organ, and so that would be better interpreted as expert organ, because an expert organ is somebody who carries out but does not make or command -- it's a person who seeks technical solutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No further explanation. Do you confirm that you said you're an expert organ or professional organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert organ, if you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 24367, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is a May 1994 document from Milovanovic, and you see it on the screen now, in which the main paragraph he speaks about an order, pursuant to the VRS Main Staff order, and he gives a number. The Chief of Staff had to report to the Main Staff in written form by a date on measures taken against Major Vujasin for not fulfilling his obligations towards the Main Staff. The same document gave the dead-line 20 May 1994 for submitting a report, and then he says no -- since no report has arrived on this day, he orders -- he says the Chief of Staff shall submit a statement in written form regarding the following questions. And he goes on to four questions and it has to do with carrying out -- the VRS Main Staff carrying out its obligation to the command and subordination, but at the very end of it, it says the report pursuant to the VRS Main Staff, and it gives a number of the report and the date, should be brought in by Major Vujasin personally to the Main Staff on May 31, 1994. Sir, can you give us any insight as to what this is all about? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to report to General Mladic. I had to report, and the reason was the inability to implement special tasks which the corps command was set, but I didn't even know that the Main Staff was asking this for the implementation of some tasks. Something cannot be done if it cannot be done. The main thing was to secure movement towards the positions, securing the movement. This was in 1994. That's when this was. So the equipment was used up. We didn't have spare parts. There was firing. There was a lack of fuel, so you could not carry out the task with the assets that you had at your disposal. So in that way, I endangered myself and was exposed to having to go and report back because of all of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you're going to have an opportunity to talk further about this, but I just want to note at the bottom in that last paragraph it cites order strictly confidential 7/13-26.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we now go to 65 ter 24366, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So now we have at the top 7-13 -- excuse me, 7/13-26, and this appears to be an order that was earlier than the one we just saw, and let's go through this. In the first paragraph it talks about conclusions from the consultations with the engineering command of the VRS and personal inspection and under number 1 the conclusion is engineering machines and motor vehicles are maximally and rationally used for construction of roads and other facilities for social political communities and companies and firms or for individuals. Number 2, construction work is conducted farther away from the front line and is not related to combat. 3, construction works are usually conducted without any economical gain usually even for free. 4, certain construction works for individuals or owners of private businesses are usually the source of gossiping at a very high -- a very high and responsible officers. And 5, intensive exploitation of engineering --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Ms. West please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And number 5, exploitation of engineering machines and lack of money caused a very high per cent of engineering machines that are not working to overcome the problems. So these are the conclusions made by Milovanovic, and then he orders, forbids commanders to work for social political communities of more than 10 kilometres from the front lines. And then number 2, engineering units shall strictly be used only for combat activities. And if we skip to number 4, he then orders the chief of engineering and the chief of planning shall do some inspections regarding construction, regarding the regularity of contracts and payments, and they should deliver a report to me on May 15th. Now, at the time you were the chief of engineering; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this report he refers to is the report that you were supposed to give him one month later that he complained about; right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That was something else. This is something else -- else. Separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was about to ask that, Ms. West. The previous document refers to the number, but it's dated as 15th of March, 1994, while this is April document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was about to ask him the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It appears that the same number's here but we have different dates. Are you telling us that there were two separate problems, one that is articulated in this piece of paper and a separate one that was articulated in the earlier document?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are two different concepts, and different papers, meaning two different, I can say. I am familiar with this document originally, the machinery or the engineering machines should be used for the purposes of the military and not for the needs of the socio-political community. So this particularly referred to the VRS units in Bosnian Krajina around Novi Prijedor and Banja Luka, in that area, Brcko and so on and so forth, rather, in Bijeljina, because work has -- life began to function already and the equipment was not being active or used at the front. So that's why it was used elsewhere. The equipment that was in the army was confiscated. It was mobilised, and it was a pity for it to be at a standstill if there were other things for it to do, so that's why it was going on this economic basis. And on the basis of the document -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continue --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No. You say that this is later, so it was at a point where --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This -- well, let's keep these two documents separate if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know the dates, but I didn't know -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So this document is dated in 1994, and you just described some issues that were going on later in the war or in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we have 24346, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is earlier in the war, September of 1992. And we should have both the B/C/S and the English of this. And again it's a National Security Service official note, and if we can go to page 2 of the English. It's page 1 of the B/C/S. This is information received, some of it including information regarding your unit. Now, the top of page 2 in the English, they've received information that lieutenant-colonel who was the brigade commander, Goljanin, that the people of Rajlovac respect and value him but the problem is that the situation in the brigade was chaotic when he arrived, and when he took it over from Vujasin, who is a very destructive man and a demigod. Lieutenant-Colonel Goljanin has big problems at this moment to correct everything that was wrong since the obvious looting and illegal gain had priority over combat activities. And you can see that in the B/C/S. And it gives an example with a person named Captain Kablar and then Sergeant Brezo. Are you familiar with these people?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have know Goljanin. I don't know which other captain you mean here.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Captain Kablar.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know him. Captain Veljancic. Yes, I know these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Were you aware of the allegations of looting and illegal gain as referenced here under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was aware of that, yes. Can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could not have been prevented. People were left without anything anywhere. A truck of goods would be stolen, and somebody would just get lost with the truck and the goods. These things did happen. It could not be prevented, and if you tried to prevent it, you would enter into conflicts. I can see here that I was accused of being a destructive person, but it means this could not have been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It means you knew about it but you didn't do anything about it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in a position to prevent such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 24345, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another September 1992 National Security Service document, and it's September 23rd, 1992, and it's a short document. If we can go to the second page on both for the relevant portion. And in this document it speaks about a number of people, you being one of them, and in the fourth paragraph it says Captain First Class Vujasin, known for his -- I think this should be demagoguery and destructiveness seems to have been transferred to the general satisfaction of the Serbian troops in Rajlovac. Sir, this is dated September of 1992. Were you transferred in September of 1992 or did you stay on for a while?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned in the beginning that I reported to the corps command on the 15th of September and that was when I became the expert organ in the corps command, and now this -- I was in the corps command according to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we go back to your statement, apologies for the moving around and maybe I can just say this, it's paragraph 41 of your statement, and earlier you had testified that you left in September, but in paragraph 41, you comment on a document, P1195, and you say that December 12, 1992, I was replaced by Milos Goljanin as commander of the Rajlovac brigade. So should we understand that between September and December of 1992 you still remained in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation is a problem. The -- the original does not state that. I can read it. Paragraph 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where are we?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're in paragraph 41 of his statement, Your Honour, D2686 in which he discusses the time-frame of his period of time in the Rajlovac brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document bears that number but that doesn't mean that the change occurred on that date.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, if that's the objection that can be done in redirect but my question regards this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll come back to the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want some clarification, sir. There is some suggestion that you left in September or some suggestion you left in December. When did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to my duty in the corps command on the 15th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 1D03259, please. This is the Bozic statement that we -- that we spoke about yesterday -- that the Court saw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, while we wait for that, can you tell us why you were transferred?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the corps command. The corps command was empty. There were no seniors officers --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question's different.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- expert officers. Why I was transferred? In order to man the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 17258, please. This seems to be the incorrect document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before doing so, can we go back to 65 ter 24345.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked the witness about his transfer, but I'm not sure he read out the remainder of that passage, and I would like him to comment, make a comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Next page, probably. Yes. You were read out -- you heard the penultimate paragraph, but the paragraph following that reads like this: "The opinion of large number of troops from the Rajlovac garrison is that the mentioned Mihajlo Vujasin is a man who obstructed many an action. For example, the mopping up of Sokolje and Brijesce hill, that he is directly answerable for the troops of TO, BiH getting as near as the garrison gates, et cetera. (redacted) (redacted) He also found out unofficially that he was transferred to Lukavica." Do you have any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? It's just a question of whether this sensitive matter should be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am a man made according to a different measure. I am not someone who accords with the measure of other people. What was happening at the time were these Serbian houses were being freed. In my opinion, even now I think that there was no need for us to expose ourselves to death and getting killed, and this applied to the other side as well. This was Muslim territory and response to pressure and requests from the population which escaped or fled from Sokolje needed to organise the army and to have the people returned. However, those people who came from -- down from up there, who came down from up there were taken to the barracks, and then they staged an uprising at the barracks that I was a demagogue, that I was not on their side, and so on and so forth. So that was this main reason. And they exerted the most pressure for their houses, their villages, furniture and everything else that was up there to be liberated and for them to just sit back and behave like gentlemen. So that was that reason, and then the easiest thing is to declare someone a demagogue. I can continue. And then once Goljanin came a month or two later he wanted to return those positions that were lost in the beginning and he did that but he did have 13 people who were killed, and he personally had to leave the barracks because there was a threat of him also succumbing to the negative influence and for something bad to happen to him. So therefore this is not what it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is the statement that you obstructed many an action, for example, the mopping up of Sokolje and Brijesce hill. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ye. Well, yes. I was not inclined to be going towards those people. This is something that would have required a lot of casualties of innocent people. When you go somewhere, it means the civilians and the soldiers would become casualties and the effect would be not much. So there was practically no need. There was practically no justification for such an action for this act.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I add to the transcript? 32, line 22, they were taken to the barracks, but the witness said they fled to the barracks. And on page 33, the witness said there are civilian casualties on both sides, both national or ethnic communities, civilians on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Vujasin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this paragraph that we just spoke of, this village of Sokolje, this is the same village that you spoke about earlier today. This is the village that you said you were there to liberate Serbian houses; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know exactly what you mean. Exactly which part of my testimony are you referring to? Can you just specify that, please? The Serbian houses, the people who fled from up there, they came to the barracks. I don't have a map here, but I could indicate it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think we can move on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm looking at the clock. How much more would you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Only briefly, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long? I'm considering whether to take a break or just --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty minutes at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Twenty minutes. Then we'll have a break after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: But I wonder why -- why the transcript always is without translating the escaped. The witness said that people escaped. "Came to the barracks." They escaped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was the B/C/S word used by the witness? When you say "escaped," what B/C/S word did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pobegli," "pobegli."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the barracks, yes, because they were attacked right at the start, right at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So do you confirm that, Mr. Vujasin? They escaped to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do confirm to the barracks, meaning as soon as the JNA army left on the 13th of May, I think two or three days after that they were attacked. So then they had to escape, they had to leave their houses, and they came to the barracks and then they began to form that kind of refugee group. And so the barracks began to fill with refugees from Brijesce and Sokolje, those who were not in the lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's be clear. Were they taken to the barracks or did they flee, they fled to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They fled or escaped from the barracks, and they got there from the hill. In any case, they were threatened there. They were threatened up there. So then they fled or escaped, "pobegli," to the barracks. As far as they were concerned, they escaped, and as far as we were concerned in the barracks, they arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue if you wish, or if you wish, we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: One more document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can continue. 17258. I believe this is just another number for the Bozic interview we saw yesterday, but I think this will allow the correct version to come up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this is a -- this is actually a statement of Jovo Bozic to the War Department and National Security Council. We understand you know who he is. This is referenced in a paragraph 41 of your statement. We can go to page 4 of the B/C/S, page 4 of the English, and he makes some comments regarding you and your transfer and I want to share those with you and then ask you a question. It's the last paragraph in the -- in the English. Ex-Chief of Staff of the Rajlovac brigade, Kovacevic, organised parties in the offices, we drank some food, didn't perform his duty. Captain Vujasin, now Major, allowed himself to, instead of doing his duty, decide who was to be a director of high school, formed enterprises, and brought people to leading positions, gave orders on taking out the goods from Rajlovac and in that way cause conflict with civilian authorities. And if we drop down a few sentences it says because of the negligence he caused in the brigade, I personally asked for his release which took three months of persuasion with higher command. Now at page 5 of the English, page 5 of the B/C/S. Speaks on the top about the engineering unit, your unit, which was formed in the brigade under the leadership of Vujasin did not show any activity and even the work initiated by the engineer was abandoned, which again pointed to the poor work of the Captain Vujasin. Despite the order not to remove engineering equipment and working machines from the Rajlovac region without the signatures of the president of the municipality and commander of the brigade, Vujasin took most of these technical equipment unauthorised to Pale when leaving for new duty. Sir, isn't it true that at least part of the reason that you were transferred has to do with a number of the comments that we've seen in these most recent documents and has to do with your incompetence and activity in your job? Isn't at that right?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that. The reason being that my moral beliefs and the law would not allow me to accept any orders from civilian authorities. I had my guidelines provided by the corps command and it was the only thing that I had to act upon. My departure to a new position had to do with the manning of the corps command, because they were short of officers. There weren't any engineer officers there. Milos Voljevic [phoen] arrived in Rajlovac, who was appointed by General Mladic when Bozic insisted, and because they had connections with the general, and it was also done through Mirko Krajisnik and civilian structures, a new person came who replaced me. I stayed for another month and went to the corps command. From the corps command, which is a superior command, one can see problems better, and I could see all of the things that had to do with the municipal structures, and -- but I focused more on other fronts. I left the Rajlovac Brigade for another place which may have caused some revolt. It was their position that the -- the number one man in the municipality was in charge of everything and it encompassed the Muslim population in Sokolje. So the Rajlovac barracks was in between the two ethnic communities and that is why I was portrayed as that kind of person. Perhaps there's no need for me to go any further than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. West. We'll have a break. Shall we have just 20 minutes' break instead of half an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, Mr. President. I'm wondering if Ms. West is going to tender any of those documents that she was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in public session again?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Today you were asked how you knew about my position on supplying water and electricity and gas to Sarajevo, and you said that Mirko Krajisnik informed you and his brother, Momcilo, of my position. Is this the same Mirko Krajisnik that they wanted to have shot because, together with you, he was protecting Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Save for that information you received, were you also familiar with our position through the activities of the army and in public about the fact that civilians have to be -- well, were you aware of our position on providing supplies to the city through some other sources?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned it from Mirko Krajisnik, and I also learned it from other people as well as through the corps command. Humanitarian assistance could never be cut off, and the utilities such as electricity had to be provided to the city because it was a lifeline for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown a 19th of September document which states that it was most likely that the Serbs cut those off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have D703, which is dated the 5th of September. I'm afraid this is handwritten. Actually, it was drafted in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out in English and you will receive an interpretation. It is my letter to Mr. Akashi, your Excellencies, whereby I thank him for his letter of the 3rd of September, and I say the following: [In English] "Extracts from my speech, to which you refer, have been reported out of context. We do not, at present, intend to impose any sanctions against the Muslims. A decision to introduce such sanctions, moreover, would not affect normal humanitarian aid provided that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is not blocking humanitarian aid destined for the Republika Srpska. Since Yugoslavia is imposing economic sanctions against us, we feel entitled to continue commercial sanctions against the Muslims. As you know, however, the policy does not cover gas, water and electricity supplies to the Muslims." [Interpretation] How does this tally with your knowledge of our position vis-a-vis these matters?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received this through our command line. The corps command received it, and the commanders conveyed that information to us. I was also aware of it. This was a 1994 document, therefore it was a developed policy which didn't necessarily need to be sent to us. It was customary to provide gas, water and electricity at all times. UNPROFOR was always there intervening whenever there were cuts. They always went to the corps command. We also wanted to make sure that the people carrying out repairs were always safe and accompanied by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the most frequent causes of such failures and cuts of supplies to the part of Sarajevo under Muslim control?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mostly due to fire and combat, or, for example, during transfer, for example, from Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D2462 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document is dated one day before the document that was shown to you. Coming from the BH command in Zagreb -- actually, from the Zagreb command to New York, to the UN.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will read it out.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is this the withdrawing -- withdrawal of weapons outside the 20-kilometre zone, TEZ?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will read it out. It was General Michael Rose writing to General Rasim Delic. [In English] "I call on you immediately to halt all military actions being taken by your forces this evening around Sarajevo in contravention of UN Security Council Resolution 836, in breach of the 8th [sic] of February 1994 airport agreement and in clear violation of the ultimatum regarding the 20-kilometre total exclusion zone around Sarajevo ... "This fighting is seriously endangering the civilian population in Sarajevo. If the fighting does not stop immediately, then I will be obliged to take all appropriate measures against your forces, including, if necessary, the use of air-strikes. A similar warning has been passed to the other side." [Interpretation] Did it ever happen that there were air-strikes against Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean based on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I mean the threat of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have the next page. On the next page we see the same letter except that it was sent to General Ratko Mladic and I was copied. You can see at the bottom, "Copy to Dr. Karadzic." Can we go to the next page -- actually, the last page. This is UN communique for the public. It says the following: [In English] "Lieutenant General Rose, commander of BH command has warned both sides immediately to halt the current serious outbreak of fighting which is taking place in Sarajevo this evening. First reports which include Cymbeline radar analysis, indicate that this fighting was initiated by infantry attacks by BH Army supported by heavy mortars firing from within the city. These initial attack were followed by a Bosnian Serb Army response using heavy weaponry. [Interpretation] The penultimate paragraph: [In English] "The BH command calls on both sides to halt the fighting immediately this fighting is seriously endangering the civilian population in Sarajevo." [Interpretation] In mid September 1994, what kind of effect did this combat have on the life of civilians in terms of electricity and gas supply?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This combat did not cause any disruption in the provision of utilities to the city. There was nothing to be gained from that so the supply continued whenever it went through the territory of Republika Srpska, especially in the direction of Sarajevo and Reljevo. There were no cuts on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What impact did it have on the proper functioning and the technicalities of the electricity grid?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a report when SFOR arrived in our Lukavica barracks. They were in contact with Major Indjic. So whenever there were failures, technical disruptions, we tried to have it fixed. I know that on a number of occasions water was cut off and other utilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 1D2462 shall be assigned Exhibit D2688. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 4, you were asked about snipers, and you mentioned that optical devices were produced in the Zrak factory.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who controlled the sites and the factory during the war?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The factory was controlled by the Muslim side in Sarajevo. It was under their control. There were no Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked whether you had sniper shooters, and you said that sights could be mounted on several different types of rifles. Can you explain to us what makes a sniper shooter? In other words, is an optical device a sight sufficient to consider someone a sniper shooter?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A sniper shooter undergoes special training. This training was carried out by the JNA. However, the VRS, specifically in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, we did not have even a single platoon of snipers. By mounting a sight on a rifle, that doesn't make a soldier a sniper shooter. I just tried to explain by saying that it improved his accuracy and visibility, but it could only focus -- it could only assist his particular actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there a separation line in your area of responsibility of your unit in an urban area and did your soldiers use sights against civilians?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were the underdog. We were always lower in terms of elevation. Even if we wanted to, and even if we had the assets, we would not have been able to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was some discussion about gas and you mentioned electricity and water. In Sarajevo, save for rifle sights, was there any other kind of war production, military production?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that there were shells that they used against us with unconventional charges. Especially I have in mind the bombs or the shells which had stronger charges in order to have a longer trajectory, which also had iron particles, fillings. Now, where they manufacture that is something I don't know, but I do know they had a number of metal industry facilities which could be reoriented towards war production easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To your knowledge, what kind of utility could be used for that kind of production?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gas and electricity. One cannot have any kind of industrial production without it, plus the raw material, that is to say metal which needed to be melted. They had ironworks which could produce such means. Before the war, I know there were such facilities that could carry out such production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What kind of electricity? What amount of electricity is needed to melt metal?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot. One needs a lot of energy and electricity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 1D20700.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we do not have a translation. A translation request was made, but there was no time to produce a translation. This is the 24th of November 1992. The staff of the Supreme Command is being informed of the activities in the research centre. Can we go to the bottom of the page. Yes. Can you look at the last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting but I have two objections here. The first is lack of translation. I'm at a complete loss on how to follow this. And, secondly, I can see that this appears to be one of those occasions in redirect where Mr. Karadzic goes through a document without establishing any foundation at all why this witness would know anything about this particular document, and it's an ABiH document, and then at the end ask, Is this consistent with your knowledge. Considering I don't have an English translation at this point I think we have to stop this questioning on the document until we get the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with Ms. West's observation. You didn't tell us or -- how this arose from the cross-examination or didn't put a foundational question to the witness, but now that witness has read the document already. But what is your question, Mr. Karadzic, not in relation to this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I laid a foundation when I asked whether we released gas and electricity, and now I'm trying to show that this could not have been manufactured had there not been electricity and gas available.
